This file covers Steps 3–6 of the project: choosing the restaurant categories,
joining businesses to reviews, the spatial join to an official boundary, and the
comparison of geographic systems. Steps 1–2 (import and New Orleans filter) are
in [`R/import.R`](R/import.R) and [`R/clean_filter.R`](R/clean_filter.R).

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
sf_use_s2(FALSE)

dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)

restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds")
reviews     <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans.rds")
```

## Step 3: Select related restaurant categories

### Individual categories

One row per business–category pair, with capitalization and whitespace cleaned.
`restaurants` and `food` are dropped from the counts because every business in
this table already carries them.

```{r categories}
restaurant_categories <- restaurants |>
  select(business_id, categories) |>
  separate_rows(categories, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(category = str_to_lower(str_squish(categories))) |>
  filter(category != "") |>
  distinct(business_id, category)

category_counts <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(!category %in% c("restaurants", "food")) |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE, name = "restaurants")

knitr::kable(head(category_counts, 25))
```

### Categories that appear together

```{r cooccurrence}
selected_categories <- c("breakfast & brunch", "coffee & tea", "cafes", "bakeries")

category_pairs <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  inner_join(
    restaurant_categories |> filter(category %in% selected_categories),
    by = "business_id",
    suffix = c("_1", "_2"),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) |>
  filter(category_1 < category_2) |>
  count(category_1, category_2, sort = TRUE, name = "restaurants_with_both")

knitr::kable(category_pairs)
```

```{r cooccurrence-wider}
# Which other categories most often sit next to the selected four?
neighbours <- restaurant_categories |>
  semi_join(
    restaurant_categories |> filter(category %in% selected_categories),
    by = "business_id"
  ) |>
  filter(!category %in% c(selected_categories, "restaurants", "food")) |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE, name = "restaurants")

knitr::kable(head(neighbours, 10))
```

### Inclusion rule

A restaurant is included if it belongs to **at least one** of the four selected
categories.

```{r inclusion}
selected_ids <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  distinct(business_id)

breakfast_coffee <- restaurants |>
  semi_join(selected_ids, by = "business_id")

tibble(
  qualifying_restaurants = nrow(breakfast_coffee),
  mean_business_stars    = round(mean(breakfast_coffee$stars), 2),
  median_review_count    = median(breakfast_coffee$review_count)
) |> knitr::kable()
```

## Step 4: Join businesses to reviews

Reviews are filtered to the selected restaurants **before** the join, so reviews
for unrelated businesses are not carried forward.

```{r join-reviews}
breakfast_coffee_reviews <- reviews |>
  semi_join(breakfast_coffee, by = "business_id") |>
  left_join(
    breakfast_coffee |> select(business_id, business_name, business_stars = stars),
    by = "business_id"
  )

tibble(
  reviews_kept          = nrow(breakfast_coffee_reviews),
  restaurants_reviewed  = n_distinct(breakfast_coffee_reviews$business_id),
  distinct_reviewers    = n_distinct(breakfast_coffee_reviews$user_id),
  mean_review_stars     = round(mean(breakfast_coffee_reviews$stars), 2)
) |> knitr::kable()

# Per-restaurant review summary, used in Step 6
review_summary <- breakfast_coffee_reviews |>
  group_by(business_id) |>
  summarise(
    reviews_in_data   = n(),
    mean_review_stars = mean(stars),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Step 5: Spatial join to official place boundaries

```{r places}
louisiana_places <- tigris::places(state = "LA", cb = TRUE, year = 2024, class = "sf")

restaurant_points <- breakfast_coffee |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) |>
  left_join(review_summary, by = "business_id") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(louisiana_places))

restaurants_with_place <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(louisiana_places |> select(GEOID, place_name = NAME),
          join = st_within, left = TRUE)

restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(city, place_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r place-mismatches}
# Restaurants whose Yelp city is "New Orleans" but whose point is not inside
# the official New Orleans polygon — inspected, not deleted.
restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(is.na(place_name) | place_name != "New Orleans") |>
  select(business_name, address, postal_code, latitude, longitude, place_name) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r place-map}
new_orleans_boundary <- louisiana_places |> filter(NAME == "New Orleans")

p <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = "grey95", color = "grey35") +
  geom_sf(data = restaurants_with_place, aes(color = stars), alpha = 0.7, size = 1.4) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C", limits = c(1, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Breakfast & coffee restaurants and the official New Orleans boundary",
       color = "Business\nstars") +
  theme_minimal()
ggsave("figures/step5_points_on_boundary.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
p
```

## Step 6: Compare geographic systems

Three systems are tested: ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, Census tracts, and the
City of New Orleans Neighborhood Statistical Areas. (Wards were considered, but
the City's ward layer metadata restricts redistribution outside its GIS
department, so they are left out.)

```{r boundaries}
# ZCTAs: national file filtered to New Orleans-area ZIP prefixes
zctas <- tigris::zctas(cb = TRUE, year = 2020, starts_with = c("700", "701"), class = "sf") |>
  transmute(area_name = ZCTA5CE20)

# Census tracts in Orleans Parish
tracts <- tigris::tracts(state = "LA", county = "Orleans", cb = TRUE, year = 2024, class = "sf") |>
  transmute(area_name = NAMELSAD)

# Neighborhood Statistical Areas (data.nola.gov, dataset exvn-jeh2)
nsa <- st_read("data/boundaries/nsa.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
nsa_name_col <- intersect(c("gnocdc_lab", "GNOCDC_LAB", "name", "NAME", "lup_lab"), names(nsa))[1]
nsa <- nsa |> transmute(area_name = .data[[nsa_name_col]])

systems <- list(
  "ZIP/ZCTA"                       = zctas,
  "Census tract"                   = tracts,
  "Neighborhood Statistical Area"  = nsa
)
```

```{r assign}
assign_areas <- function(boundaries, points) {
  points |>
    st_transform(st_crs(boundaries)) |>
    st_join(boundaries, join = st_within, left = TRUE)
}

summarise_areas <- function(assigned) {
  assigned |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
    group_by(area_name) |>
    summarise(
      number_of_restaurants   = n(),
      average_business_stars  = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
      median_business_stars   = median(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_review_stars       = mean(mean_review_stars, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_reviews           = sum(reviews_in_data, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(number_of_restaurants))
}

assigned  <- map(systems, assign_areas, points = restaurant_points)
summaries <- map(assigned, summarise_areas)
```

### Comparison table

```{r comparison-table}
comparison <- imap_dfr(summaries, \(s, system) {
  a <- assigned[[system]]
  tibble(
    `Geographic system`              = system,
    `Areas in boundary file`         = nrow(systems[[system]]),
    `Areas with ≥1 restaurant`       = nrow(s),
    `Restaurants assigned`           = sum(!is.na(a$area_name)),
    `Unmatched restaurants`          = sum(is.na(a$area_name)),
    `Smallest area count`            = min(s$number_of_restaurants),
    `Largest area count`             = max(s$number_of_restaurants),
    `Median area count`              = median(s$number_of_restaurants),
    `Areas with < 5 restaurants`     = sum(s$number_of_restaurants < 5),
    `Areas with ≥ 10 restaurants`    = sum(s$number_of_restaurants >= 10)
  )
})

write_csv(comparison, "figures/step6_geography_comparison.csv")
knitr::kable(comparison)
```

### Areas per system

```{r area-tables}
#| results: asis
for (system in names(summaries)) {
  cat("\n\n####", system, "— top 12 by restaurant count\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(
    summaries[[system]] |>
      slice_head(n = 12) |>
      mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
  ))
}
```

```{r unmatched}
# Which restaurants fall outside each system?
imap_dfr(assigned, \(a, system) {
  a |> st_drop_geometry() |> filter(is.na(area_name)) |>
    transmute(system, business_name, address, postal_code)
}) |> knitr::kable()
```

### Maps

Each map shows restaurant count per area (fill) for the system, with the
official New Orleans boundary outlined. Areas with no selected restaurants are
left blank.

```{r maps, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
map_one <- function(system) {
  b <- systems[[system]] |>
    left_join(summaries[[system]], by = "area_name") |>
    st_filter(st_transform(new_orleans_boundary, st_crs(systems[[system]])) |> st_buffer(0.02))
  ggplot(b) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = number_of_restaurants), color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "D", na.value = "grey92", name = "Restaurants") +
    labs(title = system) +
    theme_void()
}

for (system in names(systems)) {
  p <- map_one(system)
  ggsave(sprintf("figures/step6_map_%s.png", str_replace_all(str_to_lower(system), "[^a-z]+", "_")),
         p, width = 6, height = 5, dpi = 150)
  print(p)
}
```

```{r rating-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Average business stars per area against how many restaurants back that
# average — small areas sit at the extremes because they have few restaurants.
ratings_vs_size <- imap_dfr(summaries, \(s, system) mutate(s, system = system))

p <- ggplot(ratings_vs_size, aes(number_of_restaurants, average_business_stars)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ system, scales = "free_x") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Restaurants in the area", y = "Average business stars",
       title = "Area averages become unstable when an area holds only a few restaurants") +
  theme_minimal()
ggsave("figures/step6_stars_vs_area_size.png", p, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
p
```

### Which geographic system, and why

*In this section, "cafes" means all 564 selected breakfast & coffee places inside the city (breakfast & brunch, coffee & tea, cafes, and bakeries).*

#### Decision

To compare breakfast and coffee places in New Orleans, I grouped them by neighborhood (Neighborhood Statistical Areas, NSAs) rather than by census tract or ZIP code. I did this because I wanted to divide the city into meaningful areas rather than create the most granular split.

#### Criteria

**Do the boundaries match the question?** Yes. Neighborhoods are areas people already treat as one place to go, while ZIP codes were drawn for mail delivery and census tracts for counting population. Someone looking for breakfast or coffee thinks of going to a neighborhood, not to a ZIP code or a tract.

**Are the names understandable?** Yes. Labels like ZIP code 70130 or Census Tract 33 are meaningless to most readers, while neighborhood names like French Quarter are self-explanatory for most people, especially residents. Most people know only their own ZIP code, because they are asked for it on applications, but not the ZIP code of a place they want to visit.

**Are there enough cafes per area?** Yes. Compared to census tracts and ZIP codes, more neighborhoods have enough cafes to compare reliably: 15 neighborhoods have 10 or more cafes each, compared with only 11 ZIP areas and 13 census tracts.

**Are the areas too large or too small?** Neighborhoods sit between the other two. ZIP areas are too large: the largest holds 146 cafes, more than the largest neighborhood (119), so it must blend several neighborhoods together, and only 24 ZIP areas contain any cafes. Census tracts are too small: their median is 2 cafes, and 75 of 103 tracts have fewer than 5.

**How many points are unmatched?** 11 cafes are unmatched, but they aren't a loss, because they are outside the city boundary, in suburbs such as Metairie and Kenner, so including them would be pointless. ZIP codes show 0 unmatched only because their areas extend into those suburbs and include these 11 cafes, so ZIP's 0 is not a strength.

**Does the system support useful maps?** Yes, because readers recognize neighborhood names. The ZIP map has grey areas outside the city, and the tract map splits the city into so many small areas that most hold only 1 or 2 places.

**Are names and definitions documented?** Yes. Neighborhood boundaries come from the City of New Orleans open data portal (data.nola.gov, dataset exvn-jeh2), and ZIP code and tract boundaries come from the US Census Bureau.

#### Why not the others?

ZIP codes are made for mail, have numerical names, and extend beyond the city boundary. Census tracts are made for counting people, have meaningless numerical names, and are too small. I also considered wards, but excluded them because the city's ward map data restricts redistribution.

#### What it reveals

Counting the cafes in each neighborhood shows that the Central Business District has 119, the French Quarter 89, and Mid-City 31, while the other 51 neighborhoods have no more than 31 each and 325 combined. Together, these 3 neighborhoods hold 42.4% of the 564 cafes in the city. The CBD is the office district, so its cafes likely serve workers, and the French Quarter is the tourist district, so its cafes likely serve visitors.

#### What it hides

Grouping by neighborhood also hides several things. 28 neighborhoods have fewer than 5 cafes, 11 have 5 to 9, and 15 have 10 or more, so more than half of the 54 neighborhoods have unstable averages. The 11 cafes outside the city are excluded. There is no data on population, workers, or tourists, so a raw count doesn't show demand. And differences inside a neighborhood are hidden, such as one busy street versus a quiet one.

#### Future work

Future work could use census tracts in each neighborhood to better understand the spread of residents, which could help determine why some areas have fewer cafes or why people visit cafes there less frequently. It could also check whether people who rated a cafe badly have reviewed other cafes, and whether other reviews of that cafe say the same thing, to verify whether the cafe is really that bad. Another step would be to test whether more expensive cafes, or cafes in richer neighborhoods, tend to be rated better, perhaps because richer neighborhoods look cleaner and nicer. Neighboring areas with fewer than 10 cafes could also be combined, and the top 2 neighborhoods could be split further, since they hold about 37% of all cafes. Finally, it could find the best cafes for group studying, quiet Zoom calls, dates, WiFi, and more food and drink options.
